summary: The structure of a web page and its common elements, building an interface with HTML and CSS, and creating HTML forms for data entry — text boxes, radio buttons, check boxes, drop-down lists, buttons, labels and the GET and POST methods.

theory.title: The structure of a web page

blocks.content:
A web page is written in **HTML** (HyperText Markup Language). HTML uses **tags** in angle brackets to mark up the **structure and content**; most tags come in pairs — an **opening tag** `

` and a **closing tag** `

`. **CSS** (Cascading Style Sheets) describes how the elements **look**.

Welcome to the School Library

Opening hours: 8:00–17:00

blocks.content:
An **element** is a part of the page, e.g. a paragraph: `

Hello

`. It is made of an **opening tag**, **content** and a **closing tag**. An **attribute** gives extra information inside the opening tag as `name="value"`: ``.

blocks.content: Use **one `<h1>`** per page, headings in order (`h1 → h2 → h3`), **semantic elements** instead of many `<div>`s, and **`alt` text** for every image. This helps search engines and users with **screen readers**.

items.content:
`selector { property: value; property: value; }`
`h1 { color: navy; text-align: center; }`

items.title: Selectors
items.content:
- **Element**: `p { … }` — every paragraph.
- **Class**: `.note { … }` used with `class="note"` — can repeat on the page.
- **ID**: `#menu { … }` used with `id="menu"` — must be **unique**.

blocks.title: Principles of good interface design
rows: Same layout, colours, fonts and navigation on every page
The user can always find the menu and get back to the home page
Good contrast between text and background, readable font size
Not too much text, colour or animation on one page
`alt` text, labels on form fields, works with keyboard and screen readers
Works on phones and computers (`<meta name="viewport" …>`, flexible widths)

blocks.content: A part of a web page that **collects data from the user** — text, choices, passwords, files — and **sends it to a server** (or a script) for processing. It is created with the `<form>` element and contains **input controls**.

items.title: Why forms are used
items.content:
- To **get data for processing** — registration, log-in, orders, surveys, search.
- To **collect user input** in a structured way.
- To **mimic paper forms** and database records.
- **Validation** (required fields, number ranges) reduces errors before the data is sent.

items.title: The `<form>` element
items.content:
`<form action="register.php" method="post">`
- `action` — the **file / URL** that will process the data.
- `method` — **how** the data is sent: `get` or `post`.
- Every control needs a **`name`** — it becomes the key of the data sent (e.g. `email=ali@mail.kz`).

blocks.title: Form controls
rows: Choose **only one** option — all buttons in the group have the **same `name`**
Choose one from a long list, saves space
Text for a control; `for` matches the control's `id` (click the label to select it)

blocks.title: GET vs POST
rows: In the **body** of the HTTP request — not visible in the URL
Yes — can be bookmarked and shared
**Not for passwords** or personal data (stored in history, logs)
Better for passwords and personal data (use HTTPS as well)

blocks.content: Radio buttons only work as a group (one choice) when they **all have the same `name`**. Give each a different **`value`** so the server knows which was chosen. Check boxes can share a name, but more than one can be ticked.

blocks.title: Built-in validation attributes
rows: The field cannot be left empty
The text must match a pattern, e.g. `pattern="[0-9]{6}"`
The browser checks for an e-mail format

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Complete the fragment of HTML code for the Gender options of a registration form. [3]**
```html
<input type="radio" name="gender" value="male"> Male
<input type="radio" name="gender" value="female"> Female
```
`<input` for each element (1), `type="radio"` (1), the **same** `name` for each element (1).

**Q: Write the attributes for the tag `<form>` to send data from the form using the GET method. [2]**
`<form action="process.php" method="GET">` — `action` with a file name (1), `method="GET"` (1).

**Q: Write the code to create a text box for the user's city with a hint inside it. [2]**
`<input type="text" name="city" placeholder="Enter your city">` — `type="text"` (1), `name` and `placeholder` (1).

**Q: Give one argument for using HTML forms in web applications. [1]**
To **collect user input** / to get data for processing / to mimic paper or database forms.

- Forgetting the **closing tag** (`

`, ``, ``) or nesting tags in the wrong order. - Giving radio buttons **different names** — then the user can select all of them. - Forgetting the **`name`** attribute — the data from that field is **not sent**. - Using `GET` for a password — it appears in the URL. - Putting visible content in the ``. - Writing CSS without `:` and `;` (`color red` instead of `color: red;`).

questions.title: External style sheets
questions.text: A website has 30 pages. Explain why the developer should use an **external** CSS file rather than inline styles.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): one file controls the style of every page; a change is made once and applies to all 30 pages; consistent design across the site; less code in each HTML page / faster loading because the CSS is cached; separates content from presentation

questions.title: GET vs POST
questions.text: Give **two** differences between the GET and POST methods of sending form data.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each), both sides: GET adds the data to the URL vs POST sends it in the request body; GET data visible / bookmarkable vs POST not; GET unsuitable for passwords vs POST better for sensitive data; GET limited amount of data vs POST large amounts / files; GET for searches vs POST for registration / orders
scheme.model_answer: 1 GET adds the form data to the URL, whereas POST sends it inside the request so it is not visible. 2 GET can only send a limited amount of data, whereas POST can send large amounts, such as files.

questions.title: The label element
questions.text: Explain why `<label for="email">E-mail:</label>` should be used with `<input type="email" id="email">`.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): the label tells the user what to enter; for matches the id so the label is linked to the box; clicking the label selects / focuses the box; screen readers read the label — accessibility

points.criterion: Describes the field / linked via for and id

scheme.model_answer: The label tells the user what to type, and because its for attribute matches the input's id, clicking the label selects the box and screen readers can read it out.

parts.title: Why POST
parts.text: Explain why POST is more suitable than GET for this form.

scheme.mark_scheme:
